title: Do you "have" things, or are they just near you?
concept_note: Four languages, four different ways of expressing the same basic idea of possession.

entries.gloss: I have a cat. (literally: at me, there exists, a cat)
entries.note: No verb "to have" at all — possession is a location, not an action.
A dedicated possession verb (avoir), used constantly, including as a grammatical helper elsewhere.
Same structure as French — a real "to have" verb (haben), also doubling as a grammatical helper.

entries.gloss: There is a cat. (used to mean "I have a cat" when context makes the owner clear)
entries.note: No possession verb either — existence itself (いる/ある) stands in for "having," with the owner often left unsaid.

title: Does this word feel more like a "he" or a "she"?
concept_note: Three of these four languages assign every noun a gender — but the systems don't agree with each other, or even with logic.

entries.note: Two genders, largely arbitrary — no reliable ending to predict which.

entries.native: der Tisch (m), die Tür (f), das Buch (n)
entries.gloss: the table, the door, the book
entries.note: Three genders, just as arbitrary as French, plus a third option.
Three genders too, but the noun's own ending is a much more reliable clue than in French/German.
No grammatical gender at all — nouns are just nouns, full stop.

title: How does your language say "you" differently to a stranger?
concept_note: Every one of these languages marks social distance — just through a completely different piece of grammar.

entries.note: A second-person pronoun swap — pick the wrong one and it's an actual social misstep.
The exact same two-pronoun system as French, historically borrowed from it.
Same idea again, though Sie is also, confusingly, the same word as "she" and "they."

entries.native: 食べる → 召し上がる / いただく
entries.gloss: to eat → to eat (respectful) / to eat (humble)
entries.note: No pronoun swap at all — formality is instead built directly into the verb itself (keigo).

title: How much can you scramble a sentence before it breaks?
concept_note: Some languages need strict word order to know who's doing what to whom. Others barely need order at all.

entries.native: 私はりんごを食べます。
entries.note: Verb-final, but particles (は/を) mark each word's role, so order can shift somewhat since the particles carry the grammar.

entries.native: Анна читает книгу. / Книгу читает Анна.
entries.gloss: Anna is reading the book. (both orders, same meaning)
entries.note: Case endings mark subject/object directly, so word order is free to shift purely for emphasis.
Rigid verb-second rule — whatever comes first, the verb must be second, no exceptions.
Strict subject-verb-object order — reordering it doesn't just shift emphasis, it can just be wrong.
